corneille-oeuvres-marty-laveaux-t1:
Tome one opens the Marty-Laveaux edition of Corneille, issued under Ad. Regnier for a French series of great writers. The text comes from images held by the national library of France. Editors kept the old spelling and fixed only clear printer's errors.

Pierre Corneille, father of French tragedy, began as a young Norman lawyer in the 1630s. Early comedies and tragicomedies fill this first volume, works that won Paris at once. Readers meet the inventor of a new French theater of honor, wit, and will. The great tragedies still lay ahead, which makes this opening tome a record of bold beginnings.
kindred-sayings-part1:
C. A. F. Rhys Davids Englished Part One of the Kindred Sayings in 1917. The book renders the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha's discourses grouped by theme. The Pali Text Society stood behind this historic first English version.

Sayings on the aggregates, the senses, and the path fill the part. Short talks, verses, and sharp exchanges carry the Buddha's core teaching. Each group of texts circles one theme until its sense lands firm. Early Buddhism's ordered heart stands clear in these grouped discourses. The modern Sujato version sits elsewhere in the catalog for close comparison. Reading both shows how Buddhist translation grew across a full century.
quesnay-physiocratie-1768-part1:
Dupont de Nemours edited Physiocratie in 1768, gathering the writings of François Quesnay, the founder of the physiocratic school. Quesnay was physician to Louis the Fifteenth and the first thinker to model an economy as a whole system. The collection's subtitle promises the natural constitution of government most favorable to mankind.

Part 1 presents Quesnay's maxims and his famous Tableau Économique, a diagram of how wealth flows between farmers, landlords, and makers. The physiocrats held that land alone yields a true surplus, so policy should free farming and trade from restraint. Dupont's preface frames the master for new readers. The volume holds economics' first system in its founding documents. Every later school, including Adam Smith's, had to reckon with the Tableau and the doctrine built around it.
stendhal-lucien-leuwen-t1:
Jean de Mitty rebuilt Stendhal's Lucien Leuwen from rough drafts for this French edition. A note recalls that Merimee once wrote nothing to be done across the first page. The draft volumes then slept at Grenoble for fifty years before editors revived them.

Stendhal wrote the tale in 1834 and left it unfinished at his death. Young Lucien, a Paris banker's son, takes a post in a garrison town under the July Monarchy. Part one tracks his awkward schooling in love, politics, and small-town snobbery. Readers prize the book as his most charming and finely shaded novel, for all its loose ends.
